title: A level Paper 2 mock — Set A: The national and global economy
description: A full-length Paper 2 mock covering Themes 2 and 4, with a data response on a fictional middle-income economy facing a currency crisis, rising inflation and a current account deficit, and an EITHER/OR essay on demand-side policy and macroeconomic objectives. Allow 2 hours: about 25 minutes for Section A, 55 minutes for Section B and 40 minutes for Section C. Read the extracts carefully before starting Section B, use the data in every Section B answer, and include a diagram and a justified judgement wherever the question asks you to evaluate, assess or discuss.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a stock of wealth rather than a flow of income or spending?
options: A The wages a household receives in a year
B The value of a household's home and savings on 31 December
C Consumer spending on services during a year
D Government spending on the NHS during a year
questions.explanation: Wealth is a stock: the value of assets owned at a particular point in time, such as property, shares and savings. Income (A) and spending (C, D) are flows measured over a period of time. The two are linked because flows of saved income add to the stock of wealth, and wealth can generate flows of income such as rent and dividends.

questions.prompt: Which of the following has been a major cause of globalisation since the 1960s?
options: A The widespread use of capital controls to limit flows of money between countries
B Containerisation and other improvements that greatly reduced the cost of transporting goods
C A rise in average tariffs on manufactured goods agreed through the World Trade Organization
D Governments nationalising firms in order to reduce foreign ownership of industry
questions.explanation: Globalisation is the growing integration and interdependence of the world's economies. Falling transport and communication costs, such as containerisation and the internet, make it cheaper to trade and to split production across countries in global supply chains. Capital controls (A), higher tariffs (C) and nationalisation to limit foreign ownership (D) would all reduce integration. In fact, WTO negotiations have reduced average tariffs.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most likely to shift the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) curve to the left, ceteris paribus?
options: A A fall in Bank Rate
B An increase in labour productivity
C A depreciation of the pound that raises the sterling price of imported raw materials
D A fall in the world price of oil
questions.explanation: SRAS shifts when firms' costs of production change. A depreciation raises the sterling cost of imported raw materials and components, so firms' costs rise and SRAS shifts left (cost-push pressure). A fall in Bank Rate (A) mainly affects aggregate demand. Higher productivity (B) and cheaper oil (D) lower unit costs and shift SRAS to the right.

questions.prompt: Which of the following items of UK government spending is a transfer payment?
options: A The state pension
B The salaries of NHS nurses
C The construction of a new hospital
D The purchase of military equipment
questions.explanation: A transfer payment is a payment by the government for which no good or service is provided in return; it redistributes income and is not counted in GDP. The state pension is the largest UK example. Nurses' salaries (B) are current spending on a service, a new hospital (C) is capital spending, and military equipment (D) is spending on goods. B, C and D are all part of G in aggregate demand.

questions.prompt: A UK exporter agrees to sell machinery to a US customer for $2 million, with payment due in six months. Which action would allow the exporter to remove the risk that the pound appreciates against the dollar before payment is received?
options: A Buy US dollars today at the spot exchange rate
B Agree a forward contract today to sell $2 million for pounds at a fixed rate in six months' time
C Deposit the expected sterling value of the sale in a savings account
D Issue new shares on the London Stock Exchange
questions.explanation: Forward markets allow firms to fix today the price of a transaction that takes place in the future. If the pound appreciated, $2 million would convert into fewer pounds. A forward contract locks in the exchange rate, removing this risk (hedging). Buying dollars now (A) would increase, not reduce, the exporter's exposure to the dollar. C and D do not affect exchange rate risk.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why it is difficult to measure the size of an economy's output gap.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: An output gap is the difference between actual real output (GDP) and potential (trend) output, the level that could be produced when all resources are fully employed at sustainable rates. It may be positive (actual above potential) or negative.
Application and analysis (any two reasons, each developed):
- Potential output cannot be observed directly. It has to be estimated, for example by fitting a trend through past GDP or by using a production function, and different methods give different answers. The estimate depends heavily on the period used.
- Potential output itself changes. A change in productivity growth, migration or participation shifts LRAS, but this may only become clear years later, so estimates of the gap made in real time are often wrong.
- GDP data are revised. First estimates of GDP are frequently revised as more information arrives, so the measured gap changes after the event.
- Survey measures of spare capacity, such as capacity utilisation and recruitment difficulties, are based on firms' subjective judgements and may not be representative.
- The hidden economy is not fully recorded, so actual output may be understated.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: Up to 2 marks for each reason: 1 mark for identifying a valid reason and 1 mark for explaining why it makes the gap hard to measure. Maximum 4 marks. If only one reason is given, 1 further mark may be awarded for an accurate definition of the output gap (maximum 3).

questions.prompt: In 2025 a country's index of average export prices was 104 and its index of average import prices was 80 (base year 2020 = 100). Calculate the country's terms of trade index for 2025, and explain one reason why this change might worsen the country's current account balance.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Terms of trade = (index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100.
Application: (104 ÷ 80) × 100 = 130. The terms of trade have improved by 30% since 2020: each unit of exports now buys more imports.
Analysis (any one, developed):
- If demand for the country's exports is price elastic (PED greater than 1), the rise in export prices leads to a proportionately larger fall in the volume of exports, so export revenue falls.
- Cheaper imports encourage domestic consumers and firms to switch from domestic goods to imports. If demand for imports is price elastic, spending on imports rises.
- If export prices are rising because of higher domestic inflation or rising unit labour costs, the improvement reflects a loss of international competitiveness, which reduces export volumes over time.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for the formula or method; 1 mark for the correct answer of 130 (accept 130.0; no mark for 76.9, which is the formula inverted); up to 2 marks for explaining why the current account may worsen, with 1 mark for identifying the mechanism (such as price elastic demand for exports) and 1 mark for the developed chain to a fall in export revenue or rise in import spending.

questions.prompt: Explain, using the accelerator theory, why net investment may fall even though national income continues to grow.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The accelerator theory states that the level of net investment depends on the rate of change of national income (output), not on its level. Firms invest to expand their capital stock when they expect demand for their output to rise.
Application: For example, suppose a firm needs £4 of capital to produce £1 of output a year (a capital-output ratio of 4). If output grows by £10 million a year, the firm needs £40 million of new capital. If growth slows to £5 million a year, it needs only £20 million of new capital.
Analysis: When the growth of national income slows, even though income is still rising, firms need to add less to their capital stock than before, so net investment falls in absolute terms. Because the change in investment is large relative to the change in income growth, investment is volatile. The fall in investment reduces aggregate demand and, through the multiplier, may slow growth further, contributing to a downturn in the trade cycle.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for an accurate statement of the accelerator principle; 1 mark for an application, such as a numerical example or a capital-output ratio; up to 2 marks for analysis explaining why a slowdown in the growth rate (rather than a fall in income) reduces net investment.

questions.prompt: Explain how a savings gap may limit economic growth in a developing economy.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A savings gap exists when domestic saving is too low to finance the level of investment needed for a target rate of growth. The Harrod-Domar model states that the growth rate = savings ratio ÷ capital-output ratio.
Application: For example, with a savings ratio of 10% of GDP and a capital-output ratio of 4, the growth rate would be 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5%. If the population grows by 2.5% a year, GDP per capita does not rise at all.
Analysis: In low-income economies, most income is spent on necessities, so the marginal propensity to save is low. Weak or absent banking systems in rural areas also mean that savings are not channelled to firms. Low saving means few funds for investment in capital, so the capital stock grows slowly, labour productivity stays low, and incomes remain low. This keeps saving low: a poverty cycle. Closing the gap requires foreign capital (FDI, aid or borrowing), which may bring its own problems such as debt.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for defining the savings gap or stating the Harrod-Domar relationship; 1 mark for application, such as a numerical example or a feature of developing economies (low incomes, lack of banking access); up to 2 marks for analysis linking low saving to low investment, low productivity and low growth.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why an increase in net inward migration may not lead to a rise in unemployment in the UK.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Net inward migration means more people move into the country than leave it, increasing the size of the labour force. Unemployment is people of working age who are without a job, available for work and actively seeking work (ILO measure).
Application and analysis (any two, developed):
- Migrants often fill vacancies in sectors with skill or labour shortages, such as social care, health, hospitality and agriculture. They reduce structural mismatches rather than displacing UK workers.
- Migrants earn and spend incomes, raising consumption and therefore aggregate demand. Firms then employ more workers. The number of jobs in an economy is not fixed (the "lump of labour" fallacy).
- Migrants are disproportionately of working age and many come with a job offer, so they add to employment as well as to the labour force, raising LRAS and potential output.
- Some migrants start businesses, creating jobs for others.
- Migrants tend to be geographically mobile and move to where jobs are available, reducing frictional unemployment.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: Up to 2 marks for each reason: 1 mark for identifying the reason and 1 mark for explaining why it prevents a rise in unemployment. Maximum 4 marks. Answers that only assert migrants "take jobs" without explanation receive no marks.

questions.prompt: With reference to Table 1, calculate the percentage change in the value of the dral against the US dollar between 2021 and 2025, and explain one way in which this change may have contributed to the inflation shown in 2023 and 2024.
questions.context:
Marisvale: a currency under pressure (illustrative data)

Table 1: Selected economic indicators for Marisvale, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Real GDP growth (%) | CPI inflation (%) | Unemployment rate (%) | Current account balance (% of GDP) | Policy interest rate, year end (%) | Exchange rate (drals per US$1, annual average)
2021 | 4.2 | 3.1 | 6.8 | -2.1 | 2.00 | 5.00
2022 | 3.8 | 5.4 | 6.1 | -4.3 | 3.50 | 5.40
2023 | 2.9 | 7.9 | 5.9 | -6.2 | 6.00 | 6.50
2024 | 1.1 | 9.6 | 6.4 | -5.1 | 9.00 | 7.80
2025 | 0.4 | 6.8 | 7.3 | -3.4 | 8.50 | 8.10

Extract A: Boom, borrowing and the slide of the dral
Marisvale is a fictional middle-income economy of 40 million people whose currency is the dral. Its exports are dominated by processed foods, textiles and tourism. Between 2019 and 2022 a housing boom, financed by rapid growth in bank lending, pushed up household spending. Much of the extra demand was met by imports of cars, electronics and fuel, none of which Marisvale produces in significant quantities. In 2022 Marisvale's main export market, a neighbouring trading bloc, entered recession, and a severe drought cut harvests of the crops used by the food-processing industry.

The current account deficit had been financed mainly by foreign investors buying Marisvale's government bonds and lending short-term to its banks. In 2023, as interest rates rose in the USA and Europe, these investors began to withdraw their funds and the dral fell sharply. Imported fuel, which makes up around a fifth of Marisvale's CPI basket, rose in price, and trade unions in several sectors secured pay rises of 10% or more.

Extract B: The central bank responds
The Central Bank of Marisvale, which has an inflation target of 4%, raised its policy rate in several steps between 2021 and 2024 to attract capital inflows and bring inflation back towards target. Business groups complain that high borrowing costs have cut investment, and that firms with loans in US dollars have seen the dral value of their debts rise sharply. Household mortgage arrears have doubled since 2022.

Exporters report that the weaker dral has made holidays in Marisvale cheaper for foreign visitors, and tourist arrivals rose by 18% in 2025. However, textile firms say that many of their inputs, such as dyes, synthetic fibres and machinery, are imported, and that rising wages are eroding the price advantage given by the lower exchange rate.

Extract C: What next?
With the current account deficit still above 3% of GDP, the government is considering three options:
- Option 1: a temporary 15% tariff on imported cars and consumer electronics. Marisvale is a member of the World Trade Organization.
- Option 2: cuts in public spending and an increase in VAT from 15% to 18% to reduce domestic demand.
- Option 3: a five-year supply-side programme of investment in port infrastructure, vocational training and domestic renewable energy, to cut dependence on imported fuel and raise export capacity.
Some economists argue that no further action is needed, because the deficit is already narrowing as the depreciation takes effect.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: The value of the dral is the number of US dollars one dral buys, so it is the inverse of the rate shown (drals per US$1). Imported inflation is cost-push inflation caused by higher prices of imported goods and inputs.
Application: Value of the dral in 2021 = 1 ÷ 5.00 = $0.200. Value in 2025 = 1 ÷ 8.10 = $0.1235 (approximately). Percentage change = (0.1235 − 0.200) ÷ 0.200 × 100 = −38.3% (accept −38% to −38.3%). The dral depreciated by about 38%.
Analysis (any one, developed): The depreciation raises the dral price of imports. Fuel makes up around a fifth of the CPI basket (Extract A), so higher fuel prices feed directly into CPI. Higher costs of imported inputs (dyes, fibres, machinery) raise firms' costs, shifting SRAS left, which pushes up the price level. Higher prices led unions to secure pay rises of 10% or more, adding a second round of cost-push inflation (wage-price spiral). Alternatively, a depreciation makes exports cheaper and imports dearer, raising net exports and aggregate demand, which adds demand-pull pressure.
Evaluation: Not required for this question; no marks are awarded for evaluation.
Mark allocation: 1 mark for the correct method (converting to dollars per dral or using the inverse); 1 mark for the correct answer of a fall of about 38% (an answer of +62%, the change in the number of drals per dollar, scores the method mark only if correctly described as a dollar appreciation; otherwise 0); 1 mark for knowledge of imported or cost-push inflation; up to 2 marks for a developed chain of analysis applied to the extract (for example, the fuel weight in CPI or the pay rises).

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge/Application: The current account records trade in goods and services, primary income (such as interest and dividends) and secondary income (transfers). A deficit means the value of outflows exceeds inflows. Table 1 shows the deficit widened from 2.1% of GDP in 2021 to 4.3% in 2022 and 6.2% in 2023.
Analysis (any two causes, developed):
- Strong domestic demand from the credit-financed housing boom: rising household spending and wealth effects increased consumption. Because Marisvale produces few cars, electronics or fuel, the income elasticity of demand for imports is high, so imports rose faster than income (real GDP grew by 4.2% and 3.8% in 2021 and 2022).
- Recession in the main export market: lower incomes in the trading bloc reduced demand for Marisvale's processed foods, textiles and tourism, reducing export revenue.
- The drought: a supply shock reduced the crops available to the food-processing industry, cutting the volume of food exports and possibly requiring imports of food.
- Rising import prices after the depreciation in 2023 (drals per US$ rose from 5.40 to 6.50): in the short run, demand for imports such as fuel is price inelastic, so the import bill rose (the start of a J-curve).
- Primary income outflows: interest paid to foreign holders of government bonds and bank loans, which rose as interest rates rose, adds to the deficit.
Evaluation: Relative significance, for example: in 2023 real GDP growth slowed to 2.9% yet the deficit widened further, suggesting that price effects of the depreciation and the loss of exports were more important than domestic demand in that year. The drought is a temporary shock, while dependence on imported fuel and manufactures is structural. The data are annual and do not separate goods, services and income, so the causes cannot be identified with certainty.
Levels (KAA up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 2 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge or definitions; little use of the extract; analysis is assertion with no chain of reasoning.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge with some use of the data; chains of reasoning are developed for one cause or are partial for both.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied to specific figures and evidence from the extract; two clear, well-linked chains of reasoning.
Evaluation Level 1 (1 mark): A generic or unsupported evaluative comment.
Evaluation Level 2 (2 marks): A supported evaluative comment, for example on relative significance, that draws on the data.
A* answer: Selects two distinct causes, uses specific figures (the deficit rising to 6.2% of GDP, growth of 4.2% and 3.8%, the dral falling from 5.40 to 6.50 per dollar), develops each into a full chain (cause, effect on X or M, effect on the balance), and adds a supported judgement about which cause mattered more and whether it is cyclical or structural.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: A depreciation is a fall in the value of a floating currency against other currencies. It makes exports cheaper in foreign currency and imports more expensive in domestic currency. The Marshall-Lerner condition states that a depreciation improves the current account if the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports is greater than 1. The J-curve shows the balance worsening before it improves.
Application: The dral fell from 5.00 to 8.10 per US dollar between 2021 and 2025 (a depreciation of about 38%). The current account deficit widened to 6.2% of GDP in 2023 and then narrowed to 5.1% in 2024 and 3.4% in 2025. Tourist arrivals rose by 18% in 2025.
Analysis: In the short run, demand for imports and exports is price inelastic because contracts are fixed and buyers take time to switch, and demand for fuel is inelastic. Import spending in drals therefore rises and the deficit widens (2023). Over time, foreign tourists and buyers respond to lower prices, export volumes rise and domestic buyers switch away from imports, so once the Marshall-Lerner condition is met the balance improves (2024-2025). This is consistent with a J-curve. Higher net exports also raise AD, which can support growth.
Evaluation:
- Other causes: the narrowing coincides with growth falling to 0.4% and rising unemployment, so lower imports may reflect weak incomes and high interest rates (expenditure reduction) rather than the exchange rate.
- Import content of exports: textiles rely on imported dyes, fibres and machinery, so the cost advantage is partly offset.
- Inflation and wage rises of 10% or more raise domestic costs, so the real exchange rate falls by less than the nominal rate and competitiveness gains are eroded.
- Primary income: interest on dollar-denominated debts rises in drals, adding to outflows.
- Export demand also depends on incomes in the trading bloc, which was in recession, and on non-price factors such as quality.
Levels (KAA up to 6 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated knowledge; little or no reference to the information provided; analysis is descriptive.
KAA Level 2 (3-4 marks): Accurate knowledge with some use of the data; analysis develops relevant chains of reasoning but they are incomplete or one-sided.
KAA Level 3 (5-6 marks): Precise knowledge applied throughout to the data and extracts; analysis develops clear, logical chains of reasoning, with a diagram or concept (such as the J-curve) used accurately where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Generic evaluative comments that are asserted rather than supported.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Evaluation that is supported by the data and context and weighs the strength of the effects.
A* answer: Explains the J-curve and Marshall-Lerner condition and matches them precisely to the data (worsening to -6.2% then narrowing to -3.4%), uses the tourism and textile evidence to contrast sectors with different import content and elasticities, and weighs whether the improvement is really due to the depreciation or to falling domestic demand.

questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Central banks set the policy (base) interest rate to achieve price stability. Transmission mechanism: higher rates raise borrowing costs and the return on saving, and attract hot money inflows that support the exchange rate.
Application: The policy rate rose from 2.00% to 9.00% between 2021 and 2024. Inflation peaked at 9.6% in 2024 and fell to 6.8% in 2025, still above the 4% target. The dral continued to depreciate, although more slowly (7.80 to 8.10 in 2025). Growth fell from 4.2% to 0.4% and unemployment rose from 5.9% to 7.3%.
Analysis:
- Higher rates reduce consumption (mortgage costs, saving incentives) and investment (higher cost of borrowing), reducing AD and demand-pull inflation; this also cuts spending on imports.
- Higher rates attract hot money inflows, increasing demand for drals and slowing the depreciation, which reduces imported inflation.
- Credibility: decisive action may anchor inflation expectations and limit wage-price spirals.
- Costs: AD/AS analysis shows a fall in real output; the data show slower growth and higher unemployment, with mortgage arrears doubling and firms facing higher dollar debts.
Evaluation:
- Much of the inflation was cost-push (imported fuel, wage rises), which interest rates can only address indirectly and at a high cost in output: the policy may have deepened stagflation.
- Time lags of 18-24 months mean the fall in inflation in 2025 may reflect the earlier rises, so the policy may be working.
- Rates rose later than inflation (the policy rate was below inflation in 2022, 2023 and 2024, so real interest rates were negative until 2025), so the response may have been too slow.
- Rising global interest rates meant Marisvale's rates had to rise just to keep capital, limiting the effect on the dral.
- Financial stability risks: higher arrears and dollar debts could threaten banks.
- Judgement: partially effective in reducing inflation and slowing the depreciation, but at a significant cost to growth and employment, and inflation remains well above target.
Levels (KAA up to 8 marks; Evaluation up to 4 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-2 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little use of the information provided; analysis is absent or a list of assertions.
KAA Level 2 (3-5 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of the data; one or two developed chains of reasoning, which may be one-sided.
KAA Level 3 (6-8 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to the data; several clear, logical chains of reasoning covering both the intended effects and the side effects of the policy.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Generic evaluation that is asserted rather than supported.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Balanced evaluation, supported by evidence from Table 1 and the extracts, leading to a judgement on how effective the policy has been.
A* answer: Uses the data precisely (rates up 7 percentage points, inflation 9.6% to 6.8%, growth down to 0.4%), explains both the domestic demand and exchange rate channels, recognises that real interest rates stayed negative until 2025, distinguishes cost-push from demand-pull causes, and reaches a clear judgement on effectiveness relative to the 4% target and the costs incurred.

questions.prompt: Evaluate which of the options in Extract C would be most effective in reducing Marisvale's current account deficit in the long run.
questions.context:
Marisvale: a currency under pressure (illustrative data)

Table 1: Selected economic indicators for Marisvale, 2021-2025 (illustrative data)
Year | Real GDP growth (%) | CPI inflation (%) | Unemployment rate (%) | Current account balance (% of GDP) | Policy interest rate, year end (%) | Exchange rate (drals per US$1, annual average)
2021 | 4.2 | 3.1 | 6.8 | -2.1 | 2.00 | 5.00
2022 | 3.8 | 5.4 | 6.1 | -4.3 | 3.50 | 5.40
2023 | 2.9 | 7.9 | 5.9 | -6.2 | 6.00 | 6.50
2024 | 1.1 | 9.6 | 6.4 | -5.1 | 9.00 | 7.80
2025 | 0.4 | 6.8 | 7.3 | -3.4 | 8.50 | 8.10

Extract A: Boom, borrowing and the slide of the dral
Marisvale is a fictional middle-income economy of 40 million people whose currency is the dral. Its exports are dominated by processed foods, textiles and tourism. Between 2019 and 2022 a housing boom, financed by rapid growth in bank lending, pushed up household spending. Much of the extra demand was met by imports of cars, electronics and fuel, none of which Marisvale produces in significant quantities. In 2022 Marisvale's main export market, a neighbouring trading bloc, entered recession, and a severe drought cut harvests of the crops used by the food-processing industry.

The current account deficit had been financed mainly by foreign investors buying Marisvale's government bonds and lending short-term to its banks. In 2023, as interest rates rose in the USA and Europe, these investors began to withdraw their funds and the dral fell sharply. Imported fuel, which makes up around a fifth of Marisvale's CPI basket, rose in price, and trade unions in several sectors secured pay rises of 10% or more.

Extract B: The central bank responds
The Central Bank of Marisvale, which has an inflation target of 4%, raised its policy rate in several steps between 2021 and 2024 to attract capital inflows and bring inflation back towards target. Business groups complain that high borrowing costs have cut investment, and that firms with loans in US dollars have seen the dral value of their debts rise sharply. Household mortgage arrears have doubled since 2022.

Exporters report that the weaker dral has made holidays in Marisvale cheaper for foreign visitors, and tourist arrivals rose by 18% in 2025. However, textile firms say that many of their inputs, such as dyes, synthetic fibres and machinery, are imported, and that rising wages are eroding the price advantage given by the lower exchange rate.

Extract C: What next?
With the current account deficit still above 3% of GDP, the government is considering three options:
- Option 1: a temporary 15% tariff on imported cars and consumer electronics. Marisvale is a member of the World Trade Organization.
- Option 2: cuts in public spending and an increase in VAT from 15% to 18% to reduce domestic demand.
- Option 3: a five-year supply-side programme of investment in port infrastructure, vocational training and domestic renewable energy, to cut dependence on imported fuel and raise export capacity.
Some economists argue that no further action is needed, because the deficit is already narrowing as the depreciation takes effect.
questions.mark_scheme:
Knowledge: Policies to reduce a current account deficit: expenditure-switching (tariffs, depreciation), expenditure-reducing (contractionary fiscal or monetary policy), and supply-side policies that raise competitiveness and productive capacity.
Application: The deficit is 3.4% of GDP in 2025, down from 6.2% in 2023. Marisvale imports cars, electronics and fuel, which makes up about a fifth of the CPI basket. Growth is only 0.4% and unemployment 7.3%. Marisvale is a WTO member.
Analysis:
- Option 1 (tariff): raises the price of imported cars and electronics, so consumers switch to domestic goods or buy less, cutting import spending. A tariff diagram shows imports falling, government revenue rising and deadweight welfare loss.
- Option 2 (spending cuts and VAT rise): reduces disposable income and AD; with a high marginal propensity to import, import spending falls. It also reduces the budget deficit and may reassure foreign investors.
- Option 3 (supply-side programme): domestic renewable energy reduces the need to import fuel; port investment and vocational training raise productivity and export capacity, shifting LRAS right and improving non-price and price competitiveness.
- No action: the J-curve effect may continue to narrow the deficit.
Evaluation:
- Option 1: Marisvale produces few cars or electronics, so demand for imports may be price inelastic in the short run and few domestic substitutes exist; the deficit may barely fall. It may breach WTO commitments and risk retaliation against Marisvale's exports. It raises CPI at a time of 6.8% inflation. It is temporary, so it does not address the structural cause.
- Option 2: With growth at 0.4% and unemployment rising, cutting AD risks recession (negative multiplier) and higher unemployment; the VAT rise adds to inflation in the short term. It reduces imports only by reducing incomes, so the deficit returns when growth recovers.
- Option 3: Addresses the structural causes (fuel dependence, low export capacity) and is the only option that improves the balance sustainably while raising potential growth. However, there are long time lags (five years or more), uncertain outcomes, and funding problems; in the short run, investment may increase imports of machinery, widening the deficit.
- No action: risky if hot money flows reverse again; wages rising by 10% or more may erode the gain from the depreciation.
- Judgement: Option 3 is likely to be most effective in the long run because it tackles structural dependence on imported fuel and raises export capacity, perhaps supported in the short run by the depreciation already under way; tariffs and austerity treat symptoms and carry high costs at a time of weak growth.
Levels (KAA up to 9 marks; Evaluation up to 6 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-3 marks): Isolated or partially accurate knowledge; little or no application to the context; analysis consists of unconnected assertions.
KAA Level 2 (4-6 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to the context with some use of data; relevant chains of reasoning are developed but may be incomplete or cover only one or two options.
KAA Level 3 (7-9 marks): Precise knowledge applied consistently to Marisvale; clear, logical and well-linked chains of reasoning for the main options, supported by accurate diagrams where relevant.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-2 marks): Generic evaluative comments that are not supported or applied.
Evaluation Level 2 (3-4 marks): Evaluation is present and applied to the context but is not fully developed or does not lead to a clear judgement.
Evaluation Level 3 (5-6 marks): Balanced, well-supported evaluation that compares the options, prioritises, and reaches a fully justified judgement about which is most effective in the long run.
A* answer: Analyses each option with a clear chain to the current account, uses the context (WTO membership, fuel's share of CPI, 0.4% growth, 6.8% inflation) to weigh effectiveness and side effects, distinguishes short-run from long-run outcomes, and makes a reasoned final judgement that ranks the options, stating the conditions under which the judgement would change.

questions.prompt:
Answer EITHER (a) OR (b). Start your answer by writing (a) or (b).

(a) The UK economy has a negative output gap and inflation close to the Bank of England's 2% target. Evaluate whether fiscal policy is likely to be more effective than monetary policy in closing the output gap.

(b) Evaluate the view that keeping inflation low and stable should be the most important macroeconomic objective for the UK government.
questions.mark_scheme:
Option (a): fiscal versus monetary policy to close a negative output gap
Knowledge: Negative output gap (actual output below potential); fiscal policy (changes in government spending and taxation, set by the Chancellor); monetary policy (Bank Rate and quantitative easing, set by the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee); multiplier; crowding out; time lags; the zero lower bound.
Application: UK examples such as Bank Rate held at historically low levels (around 0.1%) and large-scale QE during the pandemic, alongside fiscal support such as the furlough scheme in 2020-21; the UK's high public sector net debt (close to 100% of GDP in the mid-2020s) and fiscal rules; independent central bank since 1997.
Analysis:
- AD/AS diagram: either policy shifts AD right towards full-employment output, with little inflation while there is spare capacity.
- Fiscal policy: government spending is a direct injection into the circular flow, with a multiplier effect; it can be targeted (for example, at regions or infrastructure) and capital spending also raises LRAS; tax cuts raise disposable income.
- Monetary policy: lower Bank Rate reduces borrowing costs and the incentive to save, raising C and I; lowers mortgage payments; may depreciate the pound, raising net exports. QE lowers long-term interest rates and raises asset prices (wealth effects). Decisions are quick and made by an independent committee.
Evaluation:
- Monetary policy is limited when rates are already low (liquidity trap; zero lower bound) or when confidence is weak, as banks and households may not borrow ("pushing on a string"). Fiscal policy is then more powerful.
- Fiscal policy may cause crowding out and higher debt interest costs; with high debt, the fiscal space is limited and markets may react badly (as in the gilt market turmoil of autumn 2022).
- Size of the multiplier depends on leakages; in an open economy with a high marginal propensity to import, the multiplier is smaller.
- Time lags: monetary policy takes 18-24 months to have its full effect; fiscal spending projects have implementation lags but transfers or tax cuts can act fast.
- Inflation close to 2% means the MPC can cut rates without threatening its target; the two policies are complements, and coordination matters.
- Judgement depends on the size of the gap, the level of Bank Rate, the cause of the gap (demand shock vs confidence collapse) and the state of public finances.

Option (b): low and stable inflation as the most important objective
Knowledge: Macroeconomic objectives: sustainable growth, low unemployment, low and stable inflation (UK CPI target of 2%), balance of payments equilibrium, balanced budget, environmental protection and greater equality. Costs of inflation: menu and shoe-leather costs, uncertainty, redistribution, loss of international competitiveness, fiscal drag. Phillips curve trade-off.
Application: UK CPI inflation reached around 11% in late 2022, squeezing real incomes; the Bank of England's remit; the effect of high inflation on mortgage holders, savers and those on fixed incomes; the UK's weak productivity growth since 2008.
Analysis:
- Low, stable inflation reduces uncertainty, encouraging long-term investment and therefore growth; it protects the real value of savings and fixed incomes and protects the poor, who spend a larger share of income on food and energy.
- It supports international competitiveness and the current account.
- It is a pre-condition for other objectives: a credible inflation target allows lower interest rates over time.
- Against: other objectives may matter more for welfare: unemployment has severe private and social costs (hysteresis, poverty); growth raises living standards; environmental sustainability and equality have long-term importance.
- Phillips curve: in the short run, reducing inflation may increase unemployment, so prioritising inflation can reduce output and employment.
Evaluation:
- Importance depends on the current situation: when inflation is far above target, it may dominate; when it is at target and unemployment is rising, growth and employment matter more.
- Cause of inflation matters: cost-push inflation from imported energy prices is largely outside government control, and fighting it with tight policy is costly.
- Long-run vertical Phillips curve suggests there is no lasting trade-off, so low inflation does not cost jobs in the long run.
- Low inflation is a means rather than an end; the ultimate objective is sustainable improvement in living standards.
- Deflation risks mean inflation should not be too low.
- Judgement on whether inflation control is a necessary foundation but not, on its own, the most important objective.

Mark split: Knowledge, Application and Analysis up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks.
Levels (KAA up to 16 marks; Evaluation up to 9 marks):
KAA Level 1 (1-4 marks): Isolated knowledge, often definitions only; little application to the UK economy; analysis is descriptive or confused.
KAA Level 2 (5-8 marks): Accurate knowledge with some relevant application; chains of reasoning are developed for one or two points but are partial or one-sided; diagrams may be present but are not fully explained.
KAA Level 3 (9-12 marks): Accurate knowledge applied to relevant, realistic examples; several developed chains of reasoning with appropriate AD/AS (or Phillips curve) diagrams.
KAA Level 4 (13-16 marks): Precise, wide-ranging knowledge applied throughout to well-chosen UK examples; fully developed, logical chains of reasoning with accurate diagrams integrated into the argument.
Evaluation Level 1 (1-3 marks): Generic evaluative comments, asserted rather than supported.
Evaluation Level 2 (4-6 marks): Evaluation is present and partly supported, considering alternative outcomes, but is not consistently developed or prioritised.
Evaluation Level 3 (7-9 marks): Sustained evaluation throughout that weighs arguments, considers magnitude, time lags and the state of the economy, and reaches a fully justified overall judgement.
A* answer: For (a), uses an accurate AD/AS diagram and develops both transmission mechanisms with UK evidence, then judges which policy is more effective given the specific conditions (level of Bank Rate, size of the gap, fiscal space), recognising that coordination may be best. For (b), explains why low inflation underpins growth and investment, weighs it against unemployment, growth and the environment using the Phillips curve and UK evidence, and reaches a reasoned judgement that depends on the current state of the economy and the cause of inflation.
